sentences.text: Cuspicephalus was a small pterosaur characterized by a head longer than its body and an elongated tail. This creature is distinguished by an extremely slender, triangular skull with a long pointed snout. The skull was lightweight and measured 326 millimeters in length. It was very elongated, with a height of only 55 millimeters at the back and a triangular profile.

Nearly half of the skull's length was occupied by the large nasoantorbital fenestra, a large opening in the skull roof. The rostral index, calculated by dividing snout length by maximum height, was 5.4, the highest value known for any pterosaur.

Based on a skull 32.6 cm long, Cuspicephalus had an estimated wingspan of 1.2 to 1.75 meters, which is large for a Jurassic pterosaur. Cuspicephalus likely had around thirty pairs of teeth along a straight jaw section.

The genus name Cuspicephalus is derived from the Latin word for 'cusp' due to the pointed shape of its snout and the Greek word for 'head'. The species name honors artist Gerald Scarfe, whose caricatures are characterized by frequently depicting pointed noses.

Cuspicephalus was significant as the first wukongopterid discovered outside of China, expanding the group's known geographic and temporal range. Cuspicephalus was the first wukongopterid known from outside China, whereas previously known members were five million years older.
The large size of Cuspicephalus expanded the known anatomical diversity of the group, which had previously been known only from very similar, small animals.

The fossil remains of Cuspicephalus were found in Dorset, England. The partial skull of Cuspicephalus was discovered in December 2009 by collector Steve Etches in Kimmeridge Bay, Dorset. The holotype specimen was collected by Steve Etches in December 2009 at Kimmeridge Bay on the Isle of Purbeck in Dorset, England.
Cuspicephalus was formally described in a 2013 study by David Martill and Steve Etches. The genus Cuspicephalus was named by Martill and Etches in 2011.
The species is known from the partial holotype skull MJML K1918, which lacks the jaw and teeth. There is only one recorded fossil occurrence of Cuspicephalus in the Paleobiology Database.
Cuspicephalus likely had around thirty pairs of teeth along a straight jaw section.
The species is named Cuspicephalus scarfi. The type species of the genus Cuspicephalus is Cuspicephalus scarfi.

Analysis of twelve assessable features showed that eleven matched traits of the family Wukongopteridae. The describers classified Cuspicephalus as a member of the broader group Monofenestrata. Cuspicephalus belongs to the parent group Monofenestrata.

A 2021 study placed Cuspicephalus deeply within Wukongopteridae and included it in the subgroup Wukongopterinae alongside Wukongopterus and Darwinopterus. A more exhaustive analysis published in 2015 determined that Cuspicephalus was likely a primitive monofenestrated pterosaur and specifically a member of the group Wukongopteridae.

Cuspicephalus lived during the Late Jurassic period. Cuspicephalus lived during the Early Kimmeridgian of the Late Jurassic, approximately 155.7 to 153 million years ago. Cuspicephalus lived during the Kimmeridgian stage, between 154.8 and 152.21 million years ago.

A 2023 study disputed the classification, suggesting Cuspicephalus belonged to the family Germanodactylidae instead. A 2024 paper argued that Cuspicephalus was basal within Monofenestrata and that other traditionally classified wukongopterids were actually more closely related to pterodactyloids.
The describers did not perform a cladistic analysis to determine the exact phylogenetic position of Cuspicephalus among pterosaurs.
